paper_title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual representations are largely developed for understanding, yet what makes them useful for generation remains unclear. We study this question in pixel diffusion transformers and uncover two key insights. First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility, as externally aligned semantics can be progressively lost during pixel synthesis. Second, architectural separation with specialized pixel decoders mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling, without necessarily yielding representations better suited to generation. These insights suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited. Motivated by these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG), which directly forms and exploits internal representations while retaining a plain Transformer architecture. A low-dimensional bottleneck forces generation-relevant information into a compact representation, which is then explicitly used to guide decoder generation by modifying the flow-matching target according to its induced prediction offset. RG learns clearer semantic and spatial structure while scaling efficiently in both parameters and computation. On ImageNet 256x256, RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters outperforms substantially larger pixel diffusion transformers, while RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55. RG further reaches an FID of 1.74 at 512x512 and extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.89 on GenEval and 87.1 on DPG-Bench.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Representation learning has been central theme in computer vision (Chen et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021; He et al., 2022). By transforming pixels into structured features, modern vision models have learned representations that transfer effectively across recognition tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation (Oquab et al., 2023; Siméoni et al., 2025). Yet visual representations have been developed predominantly for understanding. Whether the same notion of good representation applies to generation remains much less clear. Unlike recognition, which can discard much of the low-level image content once semantics are extracted, generation must organize global semantics and spatial structure while ultimately recovering every pixel. This raises fundamental question: what makes representation useful for visual generation? Recent generative models have increasingly borrowed representations from pretrained vision encoders. One line of work improves the latent space in which generation operates, either by aligning autoencoder latents with pretrained features (Yao et al., 2025; Leng et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2026) or by directly using such features as generative latents (Zheng et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026b; Singh et al., 2026). Another line aligns intermediate generative features with pretrained representations (Yu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Singh et al., 2025). While these approaches show that semantic representations can facilitate generative learning, they largely focus on what information representation contains. For generation, this is only part of the problem: representation may encode rich semantic and spatial structure, yet provide limited benefit if it is not properly formed for synthesis or if the generative process does not actually exploit it. We study this problem in pixel diffusion transformers (pDiTs) (Chen et al., 2025c; Yu et al., 2026), where representation learning and image synthesis take place end-to-end from raw pixels rather than through representation space predefined by an external autoencoder (Rombach et al., 2022). More importantly, JiT (Li & He, 2026) shows that competitive pixel generation can be achieved with plain Transformer, providing simple setting for examining how internal representations emerge and interact with pixel synthesis. Our analysis of this setting reveals two key insights. First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility. Aligning an intermediate JiT layer with DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023) substantially improves its semantic and spatial structure at the aligned layer. However, these gains rapidly diminish in subsequent layers as the network approaches pixel prediction. The same mismatch appears in generation: REPA (Yu et al., 2024) accelerates early training, but the baseline eventually overtakes it, while moving the alignment deeper further degrades the final FID. These results show that simply injecting stronger semantics is insufficienta representation benefits generation only when its information is preserved and remains functionally relevant to subsequent synthesis. Second, architectural separation does not necessarily improve representation for generation; it mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling across the network. natural response is to separate representation learning from pixel synthesis with an additional specialized Preprint Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers Figure 3: Architecture comparison. (a) JiT and (b) RG use patch-level input and standard Transformer blocks. JiT uses single stack, while RG conditions its decoder on the bottleneck output, which is randomly dropped during training. (c)(e) Pixel-specialized decoders take pixel-level input: patch attention with pixel-wise FFNs in PixelDiT, pixel-wise MLP in DeCo, and convolutional network with skip connections in DiP. Input tokens are noisy, output tokens are clean, and rounded squares denote the tokens output by the patch embedding or patch encoder. pixel decoder (Yu et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026). However, the decoder itself reshapes the encoder representation: its spatial modeling capacity determines what the encoder must retain, producing different balances of global semantics and spatial structure without yielding representation better suited to generation. These designs also incur substantial parameter and computation overhead. Thus, they mainly shift the modeling burden between encoder and decoder while departing from JiTs simple, scalable Transformer design. Together, these findings suggest that useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited. It should emerge through compact interface that encourages the model to organize information into concise, generation-relevant representation, while remaining tightly coupled to subsequent synthesis. Neither alone is sufficient: forcing the generator to rely on poorly formed representation can amplify unhelpful low-level information, whereas well-structured representation provides little benefit if it can be ignored. Based on these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG). RG preserves plain Transformer architecture and operates on the representation interface rather than introducing specialized pixel decoder. First, low-dimensional bottleneck between the encoder and decoder forms compact implicit latent space, encouraging generation-relevant information to be organized into concise internal representation. Second, RG explicitly strengthens the generative utility of this representation. We compare decoder predictions with and without the representation and use the resulting representation-induced velocity offset to modify the flow-matching target (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023). This increases the models dependence on the representation, while gradients through it simultaneously shape the encoder toward information useful for synthesis. The bottleneck and guidance thus play complementary roles: the former governs how the representation is formed, while the latter ensures that generation actually uses it. Pretrained representation alignment thus provides semantic scaffold, while the representation consumed by the decoder is ultimately learned end-to-end for generation. RG also shares core principle with self-distillation in self-supervised learning (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2023): the representation is bootstrapped from targets derived from the models own predictions. Whereas self-distillation sharpens the teacher distribution to induce discriminative features, RG sharpens the velocity target along the representation-induced offset, which compels the representation to encode the semantic and spatial structure required for generation (Figure 6). Figure 2 summarizes the consequences of this representation-centered design. Without introducing specialized pixel modules, RG achieves substantially stronger parameterquality and compute quality trade-off, scales consistently with model size, and develops markedly clearer semantic and spatial organization in its internal representations. On ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) 256 256, RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55, while RG-L/16 reaches 1.79 with only 459M parameters, outperforming substantially larger pixel-space models. RG further achieves an FID of 1.74 at 512512 and extends naturally to text-to-image generation, reaching 0.89 on GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) 3 Preprint Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers and 87.1 on DPG-Bench (Hu et al., 2024). These results show that effective representation learning in pixel diffusion does not require increasingly elaborate pixel decoders or ever-stronger externally imposed features. Instead, plain Transformer can learn representations that benefit generation when the representation is both properly formed and explicitly exploited.

sections.title: 2 What Makes Representations Useful in pDiTs?
sections.content: We investigate how representations in pDiTs interact with generation. Our goal is not only to ask whether representation becomes more semantic or spatially structured, but whether such improvements remain useful to the generative process. Unless otherwise specified, models in this section are base-sized and trained for 200 epochs on ImageNet 256 256 (Deng et al., 2009). We report FID-50K for generation quality, RMSC and LDS (Singh et al., 2025) for spatial structure, and linear probing accuracy (He et al., 2022) for global semantics. Appendix A.4 provides metric details. Baseline REPA-4 REPA-6 REPA-8 Figure 4: Representation quality does not necessarily translate into generative utility. REPA improves semantics and spatial structure at the aligned layer, but these gains quickly decay and do not improve final generation. REPA-k aligns layer with DINOv2 features. Does better representation quality translate into better generation? Pretrained representation alignment provides direct way to strengthen the semantic and spatial structure of an intermediate representation. Rather than asking whether alignment can improve the aligned layer, we ask what happens afterwards: does this improvement survive subsequent pixel synthesis and benefit generation? We apply REPA (Yu et al., 2024) at different layers of JiT-B/16 and track both the representation across layers and generation quality during training. Experimental Results. Figure 4 reveals clear mismatch. Aligning layer 4 substantially improves its RMSC, LDS, and linear probing accuracy, indicating stronger spatial structure and global semantics. However, these gains diminish immediately after the aligned layer as the network progresses toward pixel prediction. The same mismatch appears in generation: REPA-4 accelerates early training, but the baseline overtakes it after roughly 160 epochs and achieves better final FID (4.56 vs. 4.80). Moreover, moving the alignment deeper further degrades generation, with FIDs of 5.38 and 8.33 for REPA-6 and REPA-8. Analysis. These results suggest that later layers progressively overwrite externally imposed semantics as they specialize toward dense pixel interactions and high-frequency synthesis. This mirrors lazy aggregation in ViTs (Shi et al., 2026a): models tend to follow the shortcut their supervision permits. As per-pixel supervision is largely satisfied by local operations, pDiTs lack incentive to form and exploit high-level representations. Alignment can therefore create strong intermediate representation without making it useful to the final generative prediction; imposing it closer to the output can instead interfere more directly with pixel synthesis. Our first insight is that better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility. useful representation must remain functionally relevant throughout subsequent synthesis. Does architectural separation yield better representation for generation? natural response to the above mismatch is to separate high-level representation learning from low-level synthesis with an additional, separately designed pixel decoder. Recent pDiTs follow this route using pixel-wise MLPs (Ma et al., 2026a), convolutions (Chen et al., 2026), or pixel-level attention (Yu et al., 2026). But does such architectural separation actually produce representation better suited to generation? We compare these designs under the same training budget and x-prediction. 4 Preprint Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers Vanilla PixelDiT DiP DeCo Figure 5: Decoder design reshapes the encoder representation. Different pixel decoders induce different balances of global semantics and spatial structure in encoder. Vanilla and PixelDiT retain stronger global semantics, whereas DiP and DeCo preserve more structures but weaker semantics. Experimental Results. Figure 5 shows that pixel-specialized decoders substantially reshape the encoder representation. Their linear probing accuracy drops sharply after the aligned layer and falls below that of the vanilla Transformer decoder. At the last encoder layer, DeCo and DiP retain stronger spatial variation but weaker global semantics, whereas vanilla and PixelDiT preserve stronger semantics but poor spatial structure. Consistently, Figure 2(b) shows less spatially structured representations in PixelDiT than in RG. Table 1 shows that such specialization brings no consistent generation gain: PixelDiT roughly matches vanilla (4.26 vs. 4.17) with 55% more parameters and 67% more FLOPs, while DiP and DeCo reach FIDs of 6.09 and 9.17. Analysis. These differences reflect what each decoder can model. Vanilla and PixelDiT capture cross-patch spatial relations in the decoder, allowing the encoder to focus more on global semantics. In contrast, DeCo and DiP process patches largely independently and therefore rely on the encoder to retain spatial information. The decoder thus does not merely consume the representation; its design changes what information the encoder must retain. Together with Table 1, these results show that such redistribution does not consistently improve generation and often comes with higher parameter and computation costs. Our second insight is that architectural separation mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling rather than yielding representation better suited to generation. Moreover, this specialization departs from JiTs simple, scalable Transformer design. Table 1: Pixel-specialized decoders offer limited gains under the same training budget. PixelDiT achieves comparable FID with 55% more parameters and 67% more FLOPs, while DiP and DeCo perform worse. RG-T2I-L/16 replaces the JiT blocks of RG with the MM-JiT blocks of MiniT2I (Wang et al., 2026b), which condition on text tokens from frozen FLAN-T5-Large encoder (Chung et al., 2022). sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Pixel-Space Generation. Most diffusion models generate images in compressed latent space. Pixel-space generation directly models RGB images, avoiding the reconstruction bottleneck and preserving fine-grained details. Early work explored scalable pixel-space diffusion, flow-based generation, and autoregressive modeling (Jabri et al., 2022; Kingma & Gao, 2023; Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2024). Recent transformer-based methods improve generation through patch-level modeling, pixel-level refinement, frequency decomposition, and encoderdecoder architectures (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026). However, learning semantic representations and synthesizing dense pixels from the same raw input often slows convergence. Our method instead learns compact internal representation to guide the generative objective during training, without requiring an external encoder at sampling time. Representation Learning for Generation. Pretrained visual encoders provide semantic representations that transfer well to recognition tasks, but may discard the fine-grained information needed for image synthesis. Prior work uses these representations as diffusion latents (Yao et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026a) or aligns intermediate diffusion features with frozen encoder features (Yu et al., 2024; Shin et al., 2026). Dedicated encoderdecoder architectures also separate semantic modeling from pixel synthesis (Wang et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026). While semantic representations can improve optimization, stronger alignment does not necessarily improve generation, and external representations may be mismatched with pixel-level synthesis. Our method learns representations end-to-end under the generative objective: bottleneck encourages compact features, while representation guidance strengthens their role in generation, preserving global structure and fine-grained pixel information. Guidance in Diffusion Models. Guidance is widely used to steer diffusion models toward conditional distributions. Classifier guidance uses auxiliary classifier gradients, while classifier-free guidance combines conditional and unconditional predictions during sampling (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021; Ho & Salimans, 2022). Recent work leverages internal predictions: Internal Guidance introduces auxiliary intermediate-layer supervision and extrapolates between intermediate and final predictions during sampling (Zhou et al., 2026). RAEv2 shows that reparameterizing the REPA prediction head enables self-guidance without separately trained guidance model or an additional classifier-free forward pass (Singh et al., 2026; Zu et al., 2026). While these methods primarily guide sampling, our representation guidance modifies the flow-matching target during training using the models own representation. Gradients propagate through this representation, directly shaping both the learned vector field and the internal features used for generation. Appendix A.3 compares RG with autoguidance (Karras et al., 2024) and Internal Guidance in pixel space.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Representation Guidance (RG), which guides pixel diffusion transformers with their own learned representations. RG combines low-dimensional bottleneck with representationguided flow-matching target to strengthen the generative utility of internal features while preserving plain Transformer architecture. It achieves FIDs of 1.55 and 1.74 on ImageNet 256 256 and 512 512, respectively, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our findings highlight that useful generative representations must be both properly formed and actively exploited.
